body_references.text: The decision map in @fig-master-loop brings these questions together. It follows how we notice and interpret information, construct options, anticipate consequences, and judge how much those consequences matter. Once we choose and commit, the resulting outcomes give us an opportunity to learn.
The route in @tbl-long-form-journey expands from individual choices to interaction and the design of decision processes. Each step adds a question that the earlier parts help us answer.

When you use the map, keep the four terms in @tbl-navigation-vocabulary distinct: interpreting what something means, predicting an outcome, forming an expectation, and deciding how much the outcome matters answer different questions.
Use @tbl-reading-routes to choose a route that fits your question. The focused routes connect related chapters without requiring you to read the whole book first.

The route in @fig-part-1-route begins with a standard for a good decision: identify the feasible alternatives, consider their consequences, and clarify what matters. It then follows the actual process, from the evidence that attracts attention to the interpretation, expectations, and values that make one option seem preferable. The hiring case establishes the difference between giving reasons for a choice and explaining how it formed. A choice between job offers then shows how to construct alternatives and investigate an uncertainty that could change the decision. Later chapters examine what we notice, expect, and value before we can explain our preference.

The committee needs to improve its hiring process, but it cannot diagnose a failure merely by restating what a good decision would look like. It must identify how the actual judgment departed from that standard and what could change it. The normative, descriptive, and prescriptive perspectives in @tbl-three-questions separate these tasks and set different standards of success.

The beliefs describe what may follow; the values say how much those consequences matter. Together they support a ranking, from which the decision-maker selects a highest-ranked feasible alternative. @fig-normative-decision-loop makes these relationships visible: prediction and valuation support choice, while feedback from the outcome can inform later judgment.

The final chapter, [*Deciding With Data and AI*](42-data-driven-decision-making.qmd#separate-prediction-and-valuation), returns to @fig-normative-decision-loop to examine the division of work between AI and people. Better prediction becomes useful when it informs a feasible choice whose consequences matter. The intervening chapters explain why this requires more than a capable model: evidence can be misinterpreted, priorities can remain hidden, authority can silence disagreement, and feedback can fail to correct mistakes. Those lessons provide the basis for designing and evaluating AI-assisted decisions.

The contrasts in @tbl-seven-context-examples distinguish changes to the decision from changes to its representation. A default alters the consequence of inaction, whereas the survival and mortality descriptions present equivalent outcome data. Explaining either requires more than naming the eventual preference.

In @fig-behavioral-decision-loop, the functions can overlap, recur, become compressed through practice, or be distributed across people and technologies. The arrows show their dependencies and routes of influence.

The distinction between a standard and an explanation now gives the committee a practical task. Use @tbl-hiring-loop to identify where its process is vulnerable, then select a response aimed at that difficulty. Adding another interview will not settle a disagreement about priorities, just as agreeing on priorities will not repair unreliable evidence.
The questions in @fig-option-information can send the student back to an earlier step. A forecast may reveal a new option, and a priority may reveal a term worth negotiating.

The separate columns in @tbl-prediction-value keep forecasts open to an evidence check and values open to discussion. A weight such as “health: 30 percent” is hard to interpret until the relevant range and trade-off are specified, and uncertainty should remain visible in the entries.

To assess a proposed question or test, list its plausible answers and the action that would follow each. Then compare the expected benefit of acting on the answer with the cost of obtaining and using it. In @tbl-information-decision-branches, the pilot and timing question can redirect action; the diagnostic test, as specified, cannot.

At the less demanding end of @tbl-proportionate-analysis, low-stakes, familiar, reversible choices can rely on routines, trained intuition, or simple rules. High-stakes, novel, irreversible, strategically interdependent, or low-feedback choices deserve more explicit structure. Rationality should guide proportionate deliberation, not turn life into continuous calculation. [*Intuition and Deliberation*](08-fast-and-frugal-thinking.qmd#fast-and-frugal-thinking) asks when compressed judgment is well trained; [*Risky Decision-Making*](16-risky-decision-making-a-probability-is-not-yet-a-feeling.qmd#risky-decision-making-a-probability-is-not-yet-a-feeling) develops the expected-utility detail needed when uncertain consequences must be combined.

Zheng and Meister (2025) compare estimates of sensory acquisition on the order of $10^9$ bits per second with deliberate behavioral throughput near 10 bits per second across selected tasks. The contrast in @fig-attention-bottleneck raises a question about how rich sensory signals support much slower observable responses.[^ch03-information-rates]

The selection in @fig-attention-filter determines which available signals enter conscious report and deliberate use. Yet even a perfect search could miss a consequential signal if the sensory or measurement system never captured it. Before asking whether we noticed everything, we therefore need to ask what the system made possible to notice.

Attention filters information that a sensory or measurement system first makes available. That initial sample is already partial, as the different sensory windows in @fig-sensory-windows illustrate. Jakob von Uexküll called an organism's species-specific perceptual world its *Umwelt* (von Uexküll, 1934/2010). Bees can use ultraviolet-sensitive vision, pit-bearing snakes detect radiant heating, some elephant calls contain infrasonic components, and migratory birds use geomagnetic cues (Chittka & Menzel, 1992; Gracheva et al., 2010; Payne et al., 1986; Wiltschko & Wiltschko, 2005).
Meetings and dashboards allocate attention before any participant begins to reason. @tbl-attention-architecture traces five design choices from what they make visible to what can be missed:
Use @tbl-05-1 to match the redesign to the failure: protecting focus addresses distraction, whereas an issue excluded from the agenda needs a route into discussion.

The first row of @tbl-two-meanings-prediction asks, in effect, **“What is producing the signals I am receiving?”** The second asks **“What is likely to happen if this option is chosen?”** Both use prior information and uncertainty, but they predict different objects and are evaluated against different evidence. In the hiring case, interpreting a quiet answer as thoughtfulness is an inference about what just happened; predicting reliable future work is a further claim. One should not silently stand in for the other.

Read the middle symbol in each row of @fig-context-b13-demonstration. Its shape is identical in the two rows, but the neighbors invite different readings. The example isolates a useful question: how much of the interpretation came from the mark, and how much came from its setting?

Consider the unfinished sentence **“At the bank, she…”** After a paragraph about fishing, *cast her line* would be a plausible continuation. After a paragraph about opening a savings account, *asked about interest rates* would fit better. The words to be continued are unchanged, but the setting changes what a good answer would be. Like the neighbors around the ambiguous symbol in @fig-context-b13-demonstration, surrounding information guides interpretation. This is useful when context clarifies a task; it becomes consequential when an assumption embedded in the question quietly guides the answer.

In @fig-perception-context-lab, the paired shafts, centre circles, and grey patches are physically identical within each comparison. The surrounding geometry or luminance changes their appearance. Measuring the target can correct the judgment without necessarily turning off the impression.

Look first at the isolated light on the left in @fig-traffic-light-color-context. What color would you call it? Now look at the upper lamp on the right. Both show the same lens, but only the right supplies its familiar setting. Does recognizing the traffic signal make the upper light seem redder?

Before reading the caption, name the animal in @fig-duck-rabbit-context. Then try to find another animal without rotating the image. The challenge is to reorganize the same marks, not discover a second hidden drawing.

Watch the upper mask in @fig-hollow-face-illusion, then compare it with the featureless hollow surface below. Does the face seem to bulge toward you? Does its apparent shape change as it turns? Try separating what you **know about the shape** from what you **see**.

Predictive-processing models differ in their scope and implementation. Some model aspects of attention through precision assignment (Feldman & Friston, 2010), but precision and attention are not interchangeable. The return path through action and sampling in @fig-predictive-processing-decision also explains why a smaller prediction error need not mean a better account of the world: the system may have sampled only evidence its model already explains.

The reference class supplies an outside starting point; the causal model explains why the present case might differ. Neither should automatically defeat the other. If only 35% of comparable launches reach that retention target, the illustrative 45% forecast in @tbl-consequence-forecast adds ten percentage points that need a reason. A validated improvement in onboarding might justify an increase; confidence in the team alone does not quantify one. [Chapter 14](14-base-rates-conditional-probability-and-bayesian-updating.qmd#reference-classes-are-judgment-calls) examines the comparison group, and [Chapter 15](15-samples-randomness-regression-and-calibration.qmd#calibration-makes-confidence-answerable) shows how to evaluate forecasts against later outcomes.

The contrasting loops in @tbl-self-fulfilling-self-defeating make “Was the forecast right?” an incomplete review question. Ask also: **Through what actions did the forecast change exposure, effort, resources, or other people’s responses?** A label such as “promising” or “unreliable” may influence the conditions under which the person will next be judged. The review must distinguish that treatment from evidence about performance under other conditions.

In @fig-expectation-loop, one pathway may operate alone, or several may combine. Attention and interpretation can mediate each pathway—for example, symptom monitoring can alter physiology, and a manager's interpretation can alter resource allocation. The key identification question is which pathway in @tbl-08-expectation-pathways changed what followed (Merton, 1948; Harris & Rosenthal, 1985; Kirsch, 1985).

In @fig-expectation-loop, one pathway may operate alone, or several may combine. Attention and interpretation can mediate each pathway—for example, symptom monitoring can alter physiology, and a manager's interpretation can alter resource allocation. The key identification question is which pathway in @tbl-08-expectation-pathways changed what followed (Merton, 1948; Harris & Rosenthal, 1985; Kirsch, 1985).

Support also has to be credible. Telling employees they are trusted while retaining every decision gives them conflicting instructions. @tbl-08-1 pairs each setting’s pathway with the support or safeguard it requires, from balanced risk information in medicine to credible authority and resources in management. A disappointing result may reflect the task, material constraints, discrimination, or luck; it cannot be used to conclude that the person failed to believe strongly enough.

Value can begin to bend before deliberate comparison. Evaluative-priming studies, for example, measure whether a positive or negative cue changes response speed to a later target. Such latency differences can reveal rapid valence activation shaped by task, semantic relatedness, attention, and goal relevance (Giner-Sorolla et al., 1999; Klauer et al., 2016; Spruyt et al., 2018). Chapter 13 examines accessibility and priming in detail; here @tbl-automatic-evaluation-stages separates the initial appraisal from the broader valuation and action it may influence.

The word “preference” can also hide differences between enjoying an outcome, feeling drawn toward it, judging it worth choosing, and acting from habit. The distinctions in @tbl-value-is-not-one-thing will matter when an action continues even though it brings little pleasure:

@fig-valuation separates the option’s features from the chooser’s state, goals, and social setting. Excitement about recognition and hesitation over family time can each express a legitimate priority; neither supplies a probability that the talk will go well. **Integral emotion** concerns the decision itself; **incidental emotion** originates elsewhere and carries over into it. Anxiety caused by a difficult morning may make the invitation feel different without changing its likely consequences.

Kenrick and colleagues (2010) instead emphasize overlapping systems. @fig-overlapping-motive-systems retains their central point: later-developing motives do not erase earlier ones. The figure uses the broader label **kin care** from later work to include concern for children and other relatives (Neel et al., 2016).

The evidence requirements in @tbl-contextual-cues-and-waiting show why arousal or neural reward responses alone cannot establish a change in intertemporal choice. A behavioral shift may instead reflect perceived time or a starting-point bias toward immediate rewards. The designs help distinguish these pathways.
Apply @tbl-07-1 to the strongest reason for accepting the invitation. A feeling may identify a benefit worth valuing, but a claim about what will happen still needs independent evidence.

The sequence in @fig-choice-blindness-swap uses abstract cards to show how the face experiment separates the original selection from the option presented for explanation. Its interest lies in the reasons offered for an undetected substitution: a participant can discuss details of the rejected face as though they motivated the choice (Johansson et al., 2005).

A decision journal supplies the separate record in @fig-narrator-learning: one entry written before outcome knowledge can rewrite memory, and another appended at a specified review point. Unlike a diary, it is organized around a decision rather than a day; unlike an after-action review, it preserves the original alternatives, assumptions, forecasts, values, context, and reasons. Later, compare that untouched entry with what happened. This comparison helps reveal which parts of the explanation were available at the time and which appeared only after the result. [Chapter 41](41-decision-hygiene-build-a-process-that-can-learn.qmd#what-a-decision-journal-is) defines the evidence base and every field; [Appendix F](../appendices/appendix-c-portable-course-tools.qmd#one-page-decision-journal) provides the portable template.

Use @tbl-rationalization-detector to turn a story into claims that can be compared with evidence. A persuasive answer to every question is still a hypothesis; it earns support when it explains observations that plausible rivals do not.
The paired judgments in @tbl-process-outcome-review show why a favorable result does not excuse a poor process, and an unfavorable result does not condemn a sound one:

We need shortcuts because time and information are limited. Some make good use of reliable patterns; others give weight to what is memorable, easy to process, or convenient to believe. The route in @fig-part-2-route connects these two possibilities to the task of checking a judgment. The chapters begin with intuitive judgment, then show how comparison and presentation affect the answer, before introducing statistical tools that make an impression testable.

The bat-and-ball response and the founder example in @fig-heuristic-substitution illustrate **attribute substitution**: the mind answers an easier question that resembles the target. The same substitution occurs when “How likely is this risk?” becomes “How easily can I picture it?” or “How well will this applicant perform?” becomes “How confident did the applicant sound?” (Kahneman & Frederick, 2002). The substituted answer may be informative. The error begins when its cue is assigned more evidential weight than it has earned.

@fig-fast-slow draws on research into controlled and automatic processing (Schneider & Shiffrin, 1977; Shiffrin & Schneider, 1977). The label **System 1** is often used for a family of fast, automatic, intuitive, low-effort, associative, and affective processes; **System 2** groups working-memory-dependent, effortful, rule-guided processes. A single task can recruit several processes, and practice can change which features dominate its performance. These are broad families of processes, not two separate brain structures. Researchers also use **Type 1** and **Type 2** to avoid implying that each family is a single system (Evans & Stanovich, 2013); this book uses the familiar System labels consistently.

In @fig-daughter-finger-counting, my three-year-old daughter uses her fingers as an external counting tool to compute 4 + 1. She had to hold the problem in mind, map numbers onto fingers, and inspect the result. The same answer later can arrive without visible counting. With suitable practice and feedback, some components of an initially effortful, rule-guided activity can become faster and more automatic.

The Stroop task illustrates the effort of overriding a practiced response. In @fig-stroop-interference-lab, name the **ink colour**, rather than read the printed word. Reading is so practiced that a colour name printed in a different colour supplies a competing response before the instructed answer is ready. People are typically slower and more error-prone when controlled attention must resolve this conflict between a fluent but task-irrelevant response and the current goal (Stroop, 1935).
The contrasts in @tbl-04-1 summarize common processing features, not two kinds of person or two fixed locations in the brain. Neither column supplies a guarantee of accuracy.

The same distinction matters when deciding what deserves protection. In @fig-affect-panda-sea-star, notice which species first draws your concern and what features prompt that response. This is a judgment about appeal; deciding how to allocate conservation funds requires evidence about what each intervention would accomplish.

The recall route in @fig-affect-availability reverses a tempting inference: if failures are common, we might expect to recall many of them, but ease of recall can also result from repeatedly displaying the same failure. A risk judgment needs to separate frequency in the world from accessibility in memory.

The representativeness path in @fig-prototype-probability produces an impression of category fit; the updating path also asks how common the category is and how diagnostic the evidence is. A convincing match can otherwise overshadow a more common explanation that looks less distinctive. For hiring, diagnosis, or investment, the cost is confusing a recognizable story with a well-supported forecast.

Use @tbl-10-1 to match the check to the shortcut, while keeping open whether a vivid case reveals something the broader record misses. One near miss cannot estimate an accident rate, but it can reveal a new failure pathway. Intuition can suggest a hypothesis; evidence must then establish how much weight it deserves.

Finding what we expected can be reassuring evidence that a model works. In @fig-belief-protection-loop, however, selective search, reading, and memory build confidence that feeds back into the same belief. That loop can keep a preferred account convincing without testing whether a rival works better.

Confirmation, motivated reasoning, and self-serving attribution differ in what they protect, but they share a process risk: search, interpretation, and explanation become easier in the direction of a preferred conclusion. The corrections in @tbl-13-1 make “be objective” testable by specifying what must be compared: rival predictions, evidence thresholds, causal standards, or situational explanations.

@fig-anchor-decoy deliberately separates **effect** from **mechanism**. “Insufficient adjustment” is not a complete definition of anchoring: anchor-consistent information can become selectively accessible, and scale use or conversational inferences can also contribute in some tasks (Mussweiler & Strack, 1999; Strack & Mussweiler, 1997). Asymmetric dominance defines the decoy relation (Huber et al., 1982). The diagnostic question is therefore first whether the context changed judgment, and then which mechanism the evidence can distinguish.

@fig-subscription-decoy is memorable because the decoy received no choices, yet its removal changed what people selected. Huber et al. (1982) provide the experimental foundation for this attraction effect.

The hiring case shows why the correction must match the comparison. More careful adjustment cannot create an estimate independent of the anchor; more discussion of the candidate cannot supply a missing work sample. @tbl-14-1 matches the diagnosed problem to a practical change informed by research on debiasing (Larrick, 2004).

In @fig-context-mechanisms, the relevant distinction is what changed: the description, the preceding cue, processing ease, or the result of inaction. The clearest tests of framing hold the other ingredients fixed and compare logically equivalent descriptions.

The rows of @tbl-disease-framing preserve the same final possibilities and probabilities. The first makes a guaranteed rescue focal; the second foregrounds a guaranteed loss. [Chapter 17](17-prospect-theory-gains-and-losses-begin-at-a-reference-point.qmd#the-prospect-theory-model) uses the example to examine how reference points and probability weighting can produce that pattern.

In @fig-assumed-choice-eggs, adding “no egg” restores an option hidden by the second question. “Would you prefer delivery this week or next week?” similarly treats purchase as settled. These are cases of **substantive reframing**: the inquiry changes which options, objectives, or causal accounts receive consideration. They deserve scrutiny even though they are not tests of equivalent numerical descriptions.

That first result could reflect a changed report without a changed memory. A second experiment therefore asked about broken glass one week later. There was none in the film, yet **16 of 50** students previously asked about “smashed” reported seeing it, compared with **7 of 50** asked about “hit” and **6 of 50** controls who received no speed question. @fig-wording-memory-study-redraw keeps the immediate estimate and later report separate.

The same care applies in management. A label such as “rightsizing” should not obscure job losses, and calling a workload a “stretch goal” does not establish that it is sustainable. The safeguards in @tbl-15-1 follow what the frame changed: restate equivalent quantities, reopen missing alternatives, or test an implied cause.

The earlier-cue route in @fig-priming-pathway helps distinguish priming from [framing](12-framing-when-the-same-facts-become-different-decisions.qmd#what-a-frame-changes): survival rather than mortality describes the decision differently, while a frightening story heard beforehand changes the mental context in which the statistic is encountered. A default, by contrast, changes what happens without action. Precise names matter because they identify different corrections.

@fig-fluency-pathway brings together several fluency literatures (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009; Reber et al., 2004). Ease supplies a signal about our own processing: a readable warning takes less effort to use, and a well-understood explanation is easier to follow. Yet the feeling alone does not reveal its cause. A claim can be fluent because it is understood, because it fits prior belief, because its complexity has been hidden, or simply because it has been repeated. Easy pronunciation has also affected risk judgments in some tasks (Song & Schwarz, 2009).

Read the evidence column in @tbl-16-1 before carrying a finding across outcomes: faster processing, a changed judgment, and changed behavior are different claims. Motivation, incentives, constraints, identity, and competing cues shape the path between them.

The two branches in @fig-probability-judgment-map answer the crucial question: who could have produced this positive result? Natural frequencies preserve those nested sets, often making Bayesian reasoning more transparent than isolated percentages (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995). They expose the denominator that the 90% sensitivity figure leaves implicit.

Return to the branch manager. If the bad quarter was two standard deviations below average and the same illustrative correlation of 0.40 applied, the model would predict the next quarter at 0.8 standard deviations below average without any managerial change. That is a visible recovery of 1.2 standard deviations. @fig-regression-conditional-shrinkage shows the corresponding geometry. The recovery can be real while its attribution to the rescue plan remains unproven. Compare the branch with similarly troubled branches, examine several earlier periods, and identify which changes the manager actually introduced. That makes room for a managerial effect while accounting for the recovery that might have happened anyway.
Each requires a different comparison, as @tbl-confidence-calibration shows. Asking a confident person to “think harder” supplies none of them.

The **planning fallacy** illustrates how optimistic forecasts can affect a project: people often construct an inside-view story of the steps that should occur while underweighting delays observed in similar projects (Buehler et al., 1994; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Underestimating the time a task needs can express overestimation of what one can accomplish in that time; an unduly narrow completion window also expresses overprecision. Planning fallacy is therefore an application, rather than a fourth form alongside those in @tbl-confidence-calibration. The **outside view** begins with a reference class and then adjusts only for differences that are genuinely predictive (Kahneman & Lovallo, 1993; Lovallo & Kahneman, 2003).

In Monty Hall, seeing two unopened doors can make staying and switching look equally promising. Yet the host’s rule for revealing a goat determines what the reveal tells us: similar-looking endings can carry different evidence. In the standard Monty Hall protocol, a knowledgeable host always reveals a goat behind an unchosen door and always offers a switch; if either goat door could be opened, assume the host chooses between them uniformly at random. Following the unchosen-door branch in @fig-monty-hall-protocol shows why switching wins with probability $2/3$, compared with $1/3$ for staying (Selvin, 1975). If the host instead opens doors or offers a switch selectively, the evidence changes. Likewise, “at least one child is a boy,” “the older child is a boy,” and a parent volunteering “I have a boy” arise from different sampling rules. The transferable question is not the puzzle answer but: **How was this information generated?**

The dated entries in @tbl-probability-forecast-ledger matter because memory rounds forecasts toward outcomes. “We knew it might fail” can describe almost any vague prior statement. A dated number, event definition, and update rule allow learning to survive hindsight.

The route in @fig-part-3-route connects uncertain outcomes to the lives in which they occur. It starts with the comparison of risky options and shows why a gain or loss depends partly on the point from which it is judged. It then examines what experience teaches us and leaves unseen, before turning to the mental accounts through which we organize gains, losses, and spending. From there, we ask why choices change as their rewards or costs move closer in time.
@fig-risky-decision-map shows the comparison: the lottery’s average utility lies below the utility of its average wealth.

A risk-preference measure seems useful because it could help predict choices beyond the task. Yet changing the task can change a person’s classification. Before using that label in another setting, we need to identify what the task measured. @tbl-risk-elicitation pairs each task with what it can reveal and what complicates the inference. A model maps choices back to a parameter, but comprehension, probability format, reference point, response mode, and noise can also affect the result.
Read @fig-prospect-theory-map from the two curves at the top to the risk attitudes below: the value of a gain or loss and the influence of its probability jointly shape the prediction.

We can now combine the two influences. Curvature describes the value of the possible gain or loss; weighting describes the influence of its probability. Crossing the gain–loss domain with the probability range in @tbl-prospect-fourfold gives four recurring patterns under commonly used parameterizations.

Many consequential decisions contain both. A physician can read trial evidence and also remember patients. A resident can see a flood map and also remember years without flooding. An investor can study a long return series and still give special weight to the market experienced during early adulthood. The independent dimensions in @fig-decision-experience-states make room for all four combinations, including having neither source. When both are present, disagreement calls for investigation; neither is automatically superior.

Hertwig and Wulff (2022) organize risk situations by asking whether description and experience are present or absent. The responses in @tbl-experience-states follow from what is missing: a selective history calls for broader evidence, while a described distribution may need a clearer, more usable presentation.

The slowly falling one-percent curve in @fig-experience-rare-event-sampling shows why an uneventful sample can coexist with a real rare-event risk. The following sections examine how selective exposure, stopping, and memory shape the experienced record.

Reviewing the four cells in @tbl-process-outcome prevents a successful result from excusing a poor process or a bad result from condemning a sound one. Hindsight, self-serving attribution, and rationalization make this separation difficult. People can sincerely explain choices whose causes they did not notice (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977; Johansson et al., 2005), so a retrospective account needs something firmer than memory to compare with.

Mental accounting describes how people organize financial activities into accounts, code entries as gains or losses, and decide what to evaluate together (Thaler, 1985, 1999). @fig-mental-accounting-map follows these operations into valuation, where the same boundary can support a goal or hide a valuable alternative.

But a notional budget can become nonfungible. Someone may reject a worthwhile theatre ticket because the entertainment budget was used on a sports event, yet buy it after an equally costly medical expense or after receiving the sports ticket as a gift. Heath and Soll (1996) used such comparisons to show category-sensitive spending. @tbl-mental-budgets reports the study's **$50 prior-expense condition**. Each entry is the percentage showing the predicted “no after a prior purchase, yes after receiving that item as a gift, yes after an unrelated expense” pattern, averaged across four unrelated-expense controls.

The two panels of @fig-mental-accounting-evidence-redraw separate when an investor closes an account from the horizon over which returns are evaluated. Choose an evaluation horizon that matches the decision horizon and still permits disciplined review.

A budget helps protect money for a purpose, yet the same boundary can make a worthwhile purchase seem unaffordable while funds sit elsewhere. The audit needs to preserve the useful protection and expose the costly restriction. Check whose goal the boundary serves, whether total cost and alternatives remain visible, and whether the chooser can revise it. A saving rule should protect a goal the household endorses; a seller benefits from a misleading boundary when it hides a cost or a feasible substitute. Use @tbl-mental-accounting-audit to reconstruct the decision twice, comparing the existing account with the alternatives and future costs that its boundary may hide:

The distinctions in @tbl-22-delay-mechanisms broaden the diagnosis to include urgent needs, subjective time, and the emotions experienced while waiting:

The distinctions in @tbl-22-delay-mechanisms broaden the diagnosis to include urgent needs, subjective time, and the emotions experienced while waiting:

Before trying to make someone more patient, check whether the way the options are described changes the comparison. The classroom mnemonic **MOST** in @tbl-most-discounting keeps four option attributes visible, so that a change in wording or scale is not mistaken for a change in patience:
The choice “€100 today or €120 in a month” hides two complete outcome streams. The fuller representation in @fig-hidden-zero-frame makes the forgone payment at each date explicit:

A multiple price list seems to turn patience into a number: at which row does a person switch from a smaller-sooner to a larger-later amount? But choosing the earlier payment could also keep an urgent bill paid or avoid a promise the person distrusts. Treating either constraint as impatience would point to the wrong remedy. The design responses in @tbl-discount-identification show what must be measured or held comparable before attributing the observed choice to time preference.
Before choosing, use @tbl-intertemporal-time-stream to sketch what each option creates before, during, and after the focal event:

In @fig-habit-loop, learning concerns how responding changes across repeated episodes. Reward or relief can encourage repetition, through which a familiar cue becomes associated with the action and brings it to mind more readily (Wood & Neal, 2007). Once established, that association can persist without a satisfying outcome each time (Wood & Rünger, 2016). This helps explain why opening the feed could become easy to repeat even on nights when it offers little enjoyment; it does not establish that every later swipe is habitual.

Lally and colleagues (2010) followed people trying to establish everyday behaviors in a consistent context. The schematic curve in @fig-habit-formation-curve represents diminishing gains in reported automaticity. The median modeled time to reach 95% of the plateau was 66 days, with estimates from 18 to 254 days among participants whose data fitted the curve well.[^ch21-plateau]

The contrast between wanting and liking in @fig-wanting-liking suggests what the student could record: how strongly the next post attracted them, how enjoyable the recent posts actually were, and when they intended and managed to stop. These observations would separate attraction, experience, and the consequence for time available to sleep.

Panels A–C of @fig-reward-prediction-error-shift compare the prediction-error patterns introduced above: an unexpected reward before cue learning, a learned predictive cue, and an omitted expected reward (Schultz et al., 1997). A small response to an expected reward means little *change from baseline*, not an absence of dopamine or pleasure. Neuronal firing, dopamine release, and experienced pleasure are different measurements (Berridge & Robinson, 1998; Mohebi et al., 2019).

**A longer wait can reduce a reward's present value.** Kobayashi and Schultz (2008) trained two monkeys with cues predicting juice after different delays. Responses to the predictive cues declined as the delay increased, consistent with the animals' preference for sooner rewards. This was a known delay, unlike the unexpected lateness in panel D of @fig-reward-prediction-error-shift. Neither condition implies that waiting longer must produce stronger motivation.

@fig-reward-uncertainty-comparison adds the interval before an uncertain outcome. The solid line represents a certain reward; the dashed line represents a 50% chance of the same reward at the same time. Under uncertainty, a sustained anticipatory response can grow during the wait. The four targets in @fig-bias-and-noise separate the location and spread of comparable judgments around an observed or accepted benchmark. **Level noise** is persistent variation in judges' average severity or generosity. **Pattern noise** concerns differences in reactions to particular cases. Estimate level noise, stable pattern noise, and occasion noise with a repeated-judgment design (Kahneman et al., 2021, ch. 16).
